subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel that I must deviate somewhat from the line of discussion which I followed yesterday. During yesterday's sitting the Minister of the Interior laid on the table rather voluminous correspondence in connection with the Seven Sisters site in Manitoba, and-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I correct my hon. friend? I sent the correspondence to the Secretary of State, who tabled it together with other documents.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The minister is quite right,
but the correspondence related principally to the Department of the Interior, and I am afraid I must read part of it in order that members of the house may have some idea as to what took place before the site was handed over to the Northwestern Power Company, a subsidiary of the Winnipeg Electric Company.
The correspondence to which I am now referring is found at page 16. First I intend to read the last part of a letter from the Minister of the Interior to the Premier of Manitoba under date of February 16, 1927, approximately two years ago. The letter is as follows:
In view of what has been outlined in the foregoing, and particularly of the fact that I understand that the company is now giving serious consideration to the desirability of abandoning the Pinawa plant (which policy we have advocated for many years, although only recently with much hope of achievement). I would inquire of you as to whether you do not consider that the present time is opportune for the province and the company to endeavour to reach some mutually satisfactory understanding covering the development of the combined Pinawa-Seven Sisters reaches which will serve the two-fold end of adding a substantial block of power to the developable resources of Manitoba, and at the same time of providing the province with a substantial block of power for its present and future needs. There are many alternative ways in which this arrangement could be effected and the above ends achieved.
I would appreciate receiving an expression of your views.
This letter was in reply to the request of the Premier of Manitoba that his government be given the lease of the Seven Sisters site.

Natural Resources-Mr. Heaps
Now I want to go a little further in the correspondence and refer to a letter written under date of June 7, 1927, from the legal department of the Winnipeg Electric Company to Mr. J. T. Johnston, director of water-powers, in Ottawa. The letter is as follows: Dear Sir,
I hereby apply for a priority permit for the right to develop power on the reach of the Winnipeg river known as "Seven Sisters" in accordance with plans which are now being prepared and will be submitted to you in the near future.
It is desirous to have the permit issued in the name of a company which is now in process of incorporation. As soon as it has advanced sufficiently- I shall furnish you with the name of the company in question, and which of course will be a subsidiary of Winnipeg Electric Company.
This is a continuation of the negotiations which have been carried on for some time with your department relative to power development at the above site.
Yours truly,
(Signed) E. Anderson,
Counsel.
Now I will refer to something which does not appear in this correspondence and which, of course, could not appear in it. About this time the Nesbitt-Thomson interests acquired four foreign-language newspapers in the city of Winnipeg, I am told, for the express purpose of educating the Polish and Ukrainian citizens of Winnipeg and the German citizens of Manitoba to the idea of private development of power resources in that province. I suppose most members of the house will know that these papers have been put up for sale, now that the purpose for which they were bought has been achieved. This fact came out during the hearing of a court case in the province of Manitoba during the last session of parliament.
Going a little further into this correspondence I find a letter dated October 28, 1927, addressed to Mr. Johnston and signed by the counsel of the Winnipeg Electric Company, who is now the president of that company. The letter is as follows:
I am informed that someone has applied for homestead rights, or right to purchase two legal subdivisions 9 and 10, section 25, township 30, range 11, east. As this land is in the vicinity of Seven Sisters falls it would be reserved for water-power purposes.
I presume that "would" should be "should."
I understand the Dominion Lands office here is to give an answer to the applicant on or before the 25th November. Perhaps you will be good enough to take this up with the proper department at Ottawa and see that the land is reserved for waterpower purposes.
I might say that the department did take it up and went considerably beyond what is contained in this communication.
Now I come to a rather more significant point. I have just read some communications which show how willing the department was to acquiesce with the requests of the Winnipeg Electric Company, and on February 6, 1928, after questions had been asked on the floor of this house and the whole matter was to be aired here, the following telegram was sent by the Minister of the Interior to Hon. John Bracken, Premier of Manitoba:
Your wire February second re Seven Sisters. No truth in report that Winnipeg Electric Railway Company is urging federal government for lease to develop Seven Sisters falls. Company's application was dated June seventh, 1927, as to which your government has knowledge. Company has not submitted any further request for action in respect to its application. Mr. Johnston expects to reach Winnipeg Monday morning in accordance with your request.
Here we have a telegram from the Minister of the Interior to the Premier of Manitoba stating that there had been no such request from the Winnipeg Electric Company when I am sure that if I had time to peruse the 750 pages of this return tabled yesterday I would find it full of correspondence similar to that I have read.
Now I go a little further. I think hon. members will remember that on June 6 last the leader of the opposition raised the question of the disposition of this power site. The matter was brought up at about ten o'clock in the evening and the minister then gave the assurance to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) that no action would be taken by him or by the government until he had consulted with the members from the province of Manitoba. He also said that if the differences had not been composed there would be no leave issued for this development. In the following correspondence which was tabled yesterday I find this communication dated at Ottawa, June 7, 1928: Dear Mr. Bracken,
I have your letter of the 31st ultimo re the Seven Sisters falls lease, together with the memorandum of statements made in your legislature about the matter.
As the matter is one that has created a great deal of interest in Manitoba and_ last night, was made the matter of comment in the house by the hon. Mr. Bennett and, in view of the fact that delay of a month or so will not injure the prospects of this development, I think it wise on my paTt to delay the issuing of the license for that time.
However, I note you have not changed your position from that taken in your former letter.

What was the date of
that letter?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: June 7. Within twentyfour hours of the minister giving his pledge to the house he writes this letter to the Premier of Manitoba, as much as to say: Do not take any notice of the pledge I gave in the House of Commons; we have something in common between us and we are going to slip it over. 1 think the house deserves a little better consideration than that. I do not know whether the Prime Minister was acquainted with this correspondence, but he was good enough to read into the records of the house considerable of the correspondence in connection with the return of the natural resources. I would be pleased to have the Prime Minister read into the records of this house the correspondence from which I have just read myself.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is inferring that there was a breach of faith on my part, I want to say to the house that I tried to indicate in my speech the action I had taken to reconcile the difference of opinion which was evident among the members at that time. As I pointed out, the lease was not issued until the end of September. There was a great deal of correspondence passing between the parties; considerable pressure was brought to bear upon me throughout the whole proceedings, and I feel that I had satisfied, as far as it was humanly possible, the objections that were raised to the granting of this lease.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I have no comment to make on what the Minister of the Interior has just said. I think the letter I have just read speaks for itself.
This action of the government has created a good deal of feeling in Winnipeg and Manitoba, and rightly so, because we have had a very hard struggle to maintain our public utilities in the * city of Winnipeg., These utilities represent a large investment and are the result of a long struggle on the part of the people of Winnipeg, and anything that is done by any government institution, either by legislative or by administrative act, is bound to create a good deal of feeling in that city.
This transaction has created a feeling of distrust in the province of Manitoba. I do not know whether or not that feeling is well founded, but I would like to read a letter written by the manager of the city Hydro to the chairman of the Ontario Hydro Commission, Mr. Magrath. This letter was dated February 8, 1928, and I will only read a brief extract from it. I think the Minister of the Interior knows who Mr. Glasco is, and I do not suppose he would impute any wrong motives to him. At the time this letter was

written I do not suppose there was any thought that this correspondence would be made public, but as this whole matter has received considerable publicity I think I can quote one or two brief sentences. This is what Mr. Glasco says:
The water-powers branch's engineers and their minister too, I believe, seem partial in every way to the private power interests in this dispute that has arisen, and I am hoping that Mr. Johnson will not be able to impress his views too strongly o,n Dr. Hogg during his sojourn in Winnipeg.
The "Mr. Johnson" mentioned in the letter is Mr. J. T. Johnston, t'he head of the water-powers branch of the Department of the Interior. On February 20 I received certain replies from the minister (Mr. Stewart) in reference to a series of questions which I had placed on the order paper. My questions were as follows:
1.	Who requested Mr. T. W. Johnston, head of the water powers branch of the Dominion government to go to Winnipeg in connection with the disposition of the Seven Sisters falls site?
2.	What instructions were given to him in the matter?
T Gn whose authority did he collaborate with Dr. Hogg?
4.	What authority did Mr. Johnston have to submit a series of questions to Dr. Hogg as to whether the Seven Sisters falls should be developed under public or private ownership?
I received the following reply from the Minister of the Interior:
1 to 4 inclusive. At the request of Premier Bracken, Mr. J. T. Johnston, Director of Water Power and Reclamation, Department of Interior, visited Winnipeg to place at the disposal ot the provincial government all physical and technical data required for the consideration ot the Seven Sisters f3.11s matter under review.
I would ask the house to pay particular attention to the latter part of this reply.
Mr. Johnston did not collaborate with Dr. Hogg other than to supply data as above mentioned, nor did he submit any questions to Dr Hogg as to whether the Seven Sisters falls should be developed under public or private ownership.
I would like to quote from the Winnipeg Tribune of Friday, February 15, 1929, with reference to the eyidence given under oath by Mr. Clubb, who was then Minister of Public Works. In this article Mr. Clubb described the first meeting with Doctor Hogg, expert of the Ontario Hydro who was with the government. Premier Bracken, J. T. Johnston of the water powers branch, Ottawa, and C. H. Attwood of the water powers branch at Winnipeg had been present. The meeting had lasted two hours and he had not conferred again with Doctor Hogg. A list of questions had subsequently been drawn up between

Natural Resources-Mr. Heaps
Doctor Hogg and Mr. Johnston for Doctor Hogg to answer, said Mr. Clubb. I would like to know who is telling the truth about this matter, the head of the water powers branch of the Dominion government, or the hon. minister?
Unfortunately I have only the ordinary allotted time in which to discuss this extremely complicated question, and my first opportunity to peruse the correspondence brought down was this morning. However, I would appeal to my Liberal friends on the other side of the house who believe in the principles which elected them to office in the year 1921. During that year this country was flooded with literature, with pamphlets and with documents pleading with the electors of Canada to turn out the Conservative party. I discovered a little book in the library which contains a series of Liberal pamphlets which were broadcast throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Broadcast by whom?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
By the Liberal party. This is what appears on the very first page:
The Liberal Party led by Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King stands for
Government of the People-
Not-by Autocrats
Government by the People-
Not-by Big Interests
Government for the People-
Not-for a Favoured Few.
On page 10 of this book the following appears:
Restoration of the control of the executive by parliament, and of parliament, by the people through a discontinuance of government by order in council and a just franchise and its exercise under free conditions.
If that was the policy of the Liberal party in the year 1921 I would like to know why they have departed from that policy to-day. If government by order in council was no good in 1921, I want to assure my hon. friends on the Liberal side of the house that it certainly is no good in 1929. Conditions between then and now have not altered so much as to make it necessary for people to alter their principles. When this matter was raised by me through a question across the floor of the bouse a couple of weeks ago on the subject of the development of the St. Lawrence waterways, we were told that big questions could not be settled by the ordinary members of parliament; that the ordinary member of parliament had not the understanding, the knowledge and the technical wisdom that the members of the cabinet had. That was the inference anyone would draw, because what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has told the members is that these technical questions should first of all be settled by the cabinet, and that when the deed was signed, the house could have an opportunity of reviewing the matter.

speechtext: I presume so. Mr. HEAPS: Then the only difference between the Prime Minister and myself is: why does the house not do it? He says that the house should not do it, and I say that the house should. One of the fundamental Liberal principles is the supremecy of parliament, not the supremacy of the cabinet. In spite of all that has been said, in spite of the good qualities possessed by many members of the cabinet, I believe there could be convened from the 230 or so members who are not in the cabinet, just as good a body of men who would understand the technical advice submitted to them as there is in the cabinet itself.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first read the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I realized, as has been pretty well established in the discussion that has taken place since, that its terms are altogether too wide. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
The hon. member himself recognized that the terms of the resolution are altogether too wide because, in his own speech as reported on page 441 of the Hansard of February 25, he said:
Someone may raise the practical objection that my resolution is too broad.
Further on, as reported on the same page, he said:
I might as well be frank and say what induced me to bring forward this resolution-it was the power situation.

natural Resources-Mr. Glen
* Having widened the terms of his resolution to include, as has already been stated, so many of the functions of the administration of the departments, he will, I am sure, after the speeches of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), recognize that it will be impossible to support his resolution in its present terms. In this matter I realize fully what was intended by the hon, member in introducing his resolution. I have a good deal of sympathy with the spirit which evidently actuates the resolution, namely, that there should be no domination of the power interests in the Dominion of Canada. I, like him, have had to fight against these in the house, not in the form of the financial interests; but I remember the old feudal system of Scotland where we had just as great an iniquity as we have in the financial situation as it exists in Canada to-day. There a head was raised which it was easy to knock. Unfortunately the financial interests of Canada constitute a hydra-headed monster so that no sooner do you hit one head than another rises, and in many cases you do not know where these financial interests have their head at all.
Having said that, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre went on to complain about the domination of the power interests and he sought to illustrate that by a particular instance. I think he will agree with me that when he was at school and took his lessons in logic he learned that when you introduce a universal premise with a particular minor premise, you cannot draw a universal conclusion. He has done this, in that the domination of these interests is the major premise, while the particular premise is the innipeg power site; and therefore draws the general conclusion that all should be abolished. I cannot agree with that.
I think, however, something will have to be said from the point of view of the members for Manitoba who took part in all the negotiations leading up to the issuance of the lease. In this I am speaking not for any group but for myself, giving my own individual opinion. May I say at the outset that I have not changed my opinion from that which I held at the inception of our agitation regarding the issuance of the lease. Some history will have to be given as to the attitude of the Manitoba members. The opposition was absolutely clear and I think it can be stated in very few words. I do not propose for one moment to enter into the correspondence of which the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) who has just taken his seat, has spoken, because I have not been able to see it. I do not think it is my particular 
function to defend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in any of his negotiations. I will speak afterwards of the meetings that we had with the Minister of the Interior, but in the present instance I wish to say that despite the implication of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) yesterday that the members from Manitoba had no right to enter into this controversy because the province had all the sovereign right and were in absolute control of their resources, nevertheless the fact must be recognized that the Department of the Interior had, if not absolute jurisdiction over those resources, at all events the disposal of them within their right. That being an acknowledged fact, we as federal members from Manitoba had to take the position that we should, if possible, give our advice to the Minister of the Interior. The Minister of the Interior, very properly I think, asked the advice of the members from Manitoba. Before that was done a round robin was signed by sixteen of the seventeen members from Manitoba and addressed to the Minister of the Interior. It read:
We the undersigned members of parliament from the province of Manitoba respectfully request that the power site in the Winnipeg river known as Seven Sisters falls be retained for the use of the government of the province of Manitoba in their own provincial hydroelectric system.
After that date it is not possible to give in chronological order all the meetings that took place. We had many meetings among ourselves as members and I can assure the house that some of them were very hectic. There were some differences between the members who sit in the southeast corner of the house as well as among those who sit in line with me. Some took one position, some another, and their opinions were expressed very strongly at those meetings. At all events, suffice it to say that after a vote had been taken among the different members from Manitoba, a letter was addressed to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) on May 15, 1928, as follows:
Re: Seven Sisters Falls Dear Sir,-The federal members representing the province of Manitoba have had before them the question of the disposal of the power of the Winnipeg river at Seven Sisters falls for some time and after thoroughly going into the matter beg to advise that their recommendation in connection with same is as follows:
1.	That the site be not disposed of but that the matter be held in abeyance until the close of the next session of the provincial legislature for the purpose of giving the legislature of the province of Manitoba an opportunity to express its opinion in connection with the disposal of the said power site or the development of it by the province of Manitoba.
2.	That the said interval would afford the city of Winnipeg an opportunity to take a

Natural Resources-Mr. Glen
referendum vote on the Question as to whether the said city desires to develop the power at said site in connection with their present hydroelectric system.	.	.3.	That in the event of the province of Manitoba deciding to develop the said power as a provincial undertaking, that they be given said right upon request.	.	,,	.4.	That in the event of the province of Manitoba deciding not to develop the said site and the city of Winnipeg having reached a decision to develop same, that the city be given the opportunity of developing said power on such terms as may be satisfactory to the government of the province of Manitoba.	.5. speechtext:
The letter expressed the
majority opinion of the Manitoba members, and was signed by myself as chairman of that meeting.
In the whole controversy which ensued, whatever may have been in the minds of others, the one dominant feature in my mind was that if the issuance of this lease was a departure from the principle of public ownership, which I with other members had been on record as supporting, then so far as we federal members were concerned, we were determined to dio all in our power to delay the issuance of that lease until the representatives of the people of Manitoba had had an opportunity of declaring themselves on the matter in the legislative assembly.
It will be noted that the letter I have just read demands that the province of Manitoba, in the first instance, shall take over the site. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) spoke the other evening of having quarrelled with many of his friends. I can tell him that he is not alone in that respect. We found after this letter had been signed by the majority of the Manitoba members in the federal house that we were bombarded right and left, and that a great many of our political friends were taking opposite views from us. The Manitoba Free Press lost no opportunity to berate us, and I felt that in self-defence it was necessary that I should state and restate in the province of Manitoba the position
we took at that time. I therefore wrote a letter to the Manitoba Free Press, and also to the Winnipeg Tribune, which I propose to put on record. It is dated June 25, 1928, and read's as follows:
Dear Sir,

I would like to re-state the position of the federal members for Manitoba in view of the issues which are being injected into the controversy, and the motives which are being ascribed to them.
When the proposed agreement with the Winnipeg Electric Railway Company was before the Minister of the Interior he naturally, and as I think, correctly asked for the views of the federal members. These power sites are at present under the control and jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. The acceptance or rejection of this agreement could at any time be the subject of discussion in the House of Commons, and in that discussion I presume even the critics, newspaper and otherwise, would not challenge the right of the representatives of Manitoba to take part. How-ever the fact is that the opinion of the Manitoba members was invited, and may I say that I am convinced no member approached this question either in the role of expert, or as a politician, giving to the latter term the sinister meaning which is intended to be conveyed by editorial writers. It was a matter of the deepest concern to every individual member. I am in a position to state, that during all the discussions which took place among the members, the political significance of any decision which might be arrived at, was not even mentioned. The whole matter resolved itself into two fundamentals which I think the members were competent to discuss, these being (first) whether the proposed agreement was in violation of the principle of public control of national resources, and (second) whether the people of Manitoba were fully seized of the proposed alienation and had had opportunity of so expressing.
As to the first there can be no doubt that only extraordinary and incontestable circumstances would warrant the transfer of the Seven Sisters power site to a private company. At the time there was nothing to indicate that the transfer of this site had ever been considered as a concrete proposal by the legislature of Manitoba, and I think it is a fair statement to make that the publication of extracts of speeches of individual members demonstrate the fact that at the time these utterances were made there was no definite proposal for the acquisition of this site. Subsequently an effort has been made to show that a shortage of power will take place by 1929, according to Mr. Anderson, K.C., although Mr. McLimont puts it at 1931, and apparently there is no doubt in the minds of any of the promoters for the electric company that there will be no difficulty in disposing of the power to the consuming public. The question naturally arises in one's mind that if private capital which is usually operated on conservative and safe bases, are willing to make this large investment assured of adequate returns then certainly the province of Manitoba should hesitate, and carefully consider the granting of a franchise which despite the safeguarding clauses as to expropriation may mean the alienation of a national resource. I, with other members, have taken the position that this imperative demand for the immediate disposal of this power site is not justified. There are factors in this matter which are

Natural Resources-Mr. Glen
being, if not ignored, at least evaded. I do not propose to refer to these at this time. So far as the majority of the federal members are concerned it is not necessary in view of their decision, but it is certainly a warrantable assumption that the transfer of the Seven Sisters site means the electric company will have the dominant control of the Winnipeg river and the development of other power sites will occur only and if the company at their sweet will decide to do so.
This brings me to the second fundamental I have referred to, whether the citizens of the province are seized of the facts and have expressed themselves. To state that is to answer it. It can be moderately stated that until the proposed agreement was submitted for completion the people generally had no idea of its purport. Since then there has been a newspaper controversy which while helpful does not reflect general public opinion. I have met Winnipeg citizens who might have been expected to take sides on behalf of the electric company protesting against the feverish activity to dispose of the power site. It is somewhat remarkable that this immediate need should develop in so short a time, and should take the form of a stampede. Those of us who sought and requested delay in order that sane and reasonable consideration should be given to a matter so important have not in my opinion exceeded our duty as members, apart altogether from our rights as individual citizens. We did not take a position antagonistic to the electric company. We did 'not assume a knowledge of the whole question, although some of us could, I think, without unduly straining our intelligence, form and express a decision on the subject matter quite as competently as those who assume the position of promoters. All we did was to counsel delay and this was done in the form of a resolution whose terms seem to have been forgotten, and which were as follows:
Then follows the letter which I have already read, and with which I shall not trouble the house again. To continue:
There is danger in the confusion of issues which have been created. There is no hostility on the part of the federal members to the proposed agreement with the electric company. As a matter of fact there is a specific declaration that m the event of the province or the city of Winnipeg refusing to develop the power site this company be given priority to any other company. There is no hostility to the provincial government. If no mandate is given by the people to the government to undertake the proposition they will suffer no loss of prestige, in fact the contrary. If the city of Winnipeg decide not to proceed to develop then the whole proposition must come back to the electric company and the consideration then of the terms of the agreement. Whatever the ultimate result we have taken the position that this whole matter should not be disposed of until some opportunity is given to the people to express their opinion. That is what we recommended. Was it an unreasonable request? The people must judge.
For these reasons I was convinced then, as I am now, that our proposal that the government of Manitoba submit the agreement to the legislature for ratification was the proper procedure.

Now I come to what has been injected into this controversy, namely, the conference which took place between the representatives of the Dominion and the province of Manitoba, an announcement regarding which was made on July 11, 1928. There will be some difference of opinion among the members from Manitoba as to the effect of clause six of that announcement. It reads:
Pending this transfer-that is, the transfer to the province of the unalienated natural resources within its boundaries-the policy of the government of Canada in the administration of the natural resources of Manitoba to be in accord with the wishes of the government of the province.
During the session of 1928 the Prime Minister announced that an opportunity would be given for a discussion with the province of Manitoba in regard to its natural resources. That assurance was prompted probably by members on this side of the house, and in particular by some of ourselves representing Manitoba constituencies. There was a resolution on the order paper dealing with the return of the natural resources of Alberta, which I will frankly say gave us some concern as to how we were to vote. It became a question whether the natural resources were to be dealt with according to the wishes and the direction of the provinces. Ultimately that resolution was withdrawn, but the Prime Minister on the floor of the house gave an undertaking that the natural resources question with the province of Manitoba would be settled at an early date, and we were satisfied.
A conference did take place for the purpose of dealing with the question of the return of the natural resources to the province of Manitoba. In my judgment that altered the position so far as J personally was concerned; and as I said at the beginning I am speaking wholly for myself. Before I became a member of this house I with many other citizens had been urging the provincial government to request the Dominion government to return the natural resources. Every government that I know of, whether Liberal, Conservative or Progressive, has from time to time demanded the return of the natural resources to the province. When the time came for a discussion between the Dominion and the province it was set forth in the announcement to which I have referred that these resources would be returned to Manitoba, and that pending their transfer the provincial government would have control and that the Dominion government would make whatever disposition of the resources the provincial authorities might desire. I think, as the Prime Minister stated yesterday, that that was an entirely reasonable thing for the province of Manitoba to ask, and I am still of that opinion.

Natural Resources-Mr. Glen
As I say, I took that position then, and I stated it to the Minister of the Interior when I saw him in Winnipeg in August last. The only modification in my view was this, that I thought the responsibility for the disposal of that power site must rest with the province of Manitoba. As a federal member, having expressed that view publicly, I was determined that the province of Manitoba should take absolute control of the disposition of its natural resources, and that it was the right and duty of the provincial government so to do.
I understand that for the meeting with the Minister of the Interior in Winnipeg in August last a number of the Manitoba members were not available, and consequently were not present. I happened to be at that meeting, and I may say it was not held in a back room. Seven of the federal members from Manitoba met the Minister of the Interior. We expressed the opinion then, as I think we will express it now, that there was no change in our attitude with regard to delay, that that attitude had not been altered in the slightest degree; but we did state what I have already stated, that in view of the anouncement made by the federal government that the natural resources would be held at the disposal of the provincial government, we must see to it that they definitely and unequivocally assumed full responsibility in the matter. If my memory serves me right, I suggested to the Minister of the Interior that no report of an3r interview with Premier Bracken was sufficient, that there ought to be an authoritative statement from the Manitoba government by way of order in council that they wished the Dominion government to issue a lease of the water-power site.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Interior did consult with seven of the members from the province of Manitoba, and he advised us of the demand that had been made by Premier Bracken and what the federal government proposed to do. That did not alter my personal opinion that I as a private citizen of the province of Manitoba will have a right to express at any time in the future, but I did take the position, as I do now, that the provincial authorities having accepted the offer of the Dominion government for the return of the natural resources -and that agreement is likely to be ratified by this parliament-they were responsible solely for the disposition of any of those resources.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Marquette ('Mr. Glen) will not be true to his principles of public ownership or true to the interests of the province of Manitoba or of liberalism so far as its natural resources are concerned, if he does not now vote to defend those principles. Manitoba and the two sister provinces in the



Natural Resources-Mr. Church
years to come will be very greatly interested in mineral development and in water-power, even though agriculture at the present time may be the basic industry there. What has kept New Ontario back for so long has been the lack of cheap light and power. Away back in 1905 Sir Adam Beck wanted to electrify the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, but was defeated in bis efforts. New Ontario was thus set back twenty or twenty-five years because the water-powers in that great country were controlled by private interests. The Ottawa Journal says of Mr. King's policy:
Government by Sidestepping
As an adroit side-stepper of issues calling for decisiveness and responsibility, the palm must go to our Prime Minister, Mr. Mackenzie King. His handling of the St. Lawrence waterway question illustrates his skill. Last year Mr. King said that nothing could be done about this problem until the Supreme Court decided the respective jurisdictions of the Dominion and the provinces in regard to water-power. In the circumstances, the obvious _ course was to get the provinces and the Dominion to agree upon a set of questions to be answered by the court. That, indeed, was what the provinces wanted. They suggested that there should be a preliminary meeting with the court, and that at this meeting an effort be made to arrive at questions which should be drafted for consideration.
That, however, didn't suit Mr. King. What did suit him was that the Justice Department should draw up a set of vague questions baffling to the proverbial Philadelphia lawyer. The result is well known. The Supreme Court held a hearing; there were long arguments by high-priced counsel; much expense-and nothing else. The court, while answering certain things that didn't much matter, left other things that did matter almost as they were. The questions, it said, were too vague.
That, however, didn't worry Mr. King. It had gained him almost a year of delay, and, what was more to his liking, it gave chance for further delay. And Mr. King took the chance. He took it in the form of deciding that there should now be a-conference. Nothing, -when you want to drag something, like a conference.
The conference that the provinces wanted last year, is to be held this year. It is to be held after the session, between Ontario and Quebec on the one hand, the Dominion government on the other. The other provinces, if they evince sufficient interest, may be let in. The conference, of course, is to be over the same old question of the ownership of power.
So Mr. King gets at least another year when he doesn't have to worry over what Canada should do about the St. Lawrence Deep Waterway. He has written a nice letter to Washington about it, telling them that until he can get this matter settled it is impossible to negotiate wih Mr. Hoover or anybody else about going ahead with the project. Truly, Mr. King missed his vocation; he should have been a diplomatist.

Not that Canada is terribly anxious about the St. LavTence Waterway. Except for Toronto, which has a pipe-dream about being a great seaport, it isn't anxious at all. That, however, isn't the point. What we are trying to show is the tortuous, circuitous, yet adroit way Mr. King has of getting out of saying Yes or No.
Yeste-rday we had a remarkable speech from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). We need not worry as to where the Liberal party stands to-day jn this matter. The official Liberal party has always been opposed to the hydro and cheap light and power, controlled and developed and owned by the people themselves. In 1905 we had just such a spectacle as we saw yesterday in the Prime Minister's speech. At that time similar speeches were being made by members of the Ross-Hardy government, who were removed from office by the people when they gave away the last concession of 20,000 feet of water in the Niagara, The day before yesterday the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) also made a speech in this house, showing that he had not played the game with the Manitoba members.
Last May I was prepared to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of raising this very question of the Seven Sisters site. On that occasion I moved for the production of papers, letters and so forth regarding the Seven Sisters, falls, and I also requested at the same time the correspondence with reference to the Slave falls. The Minister of the Interior, in reply to that motion, is reported:
Hon. Mr. Stewart:
A great deal of corespondence would have to be brought down if the motion was passed as it stands, and I am informed that a great deal of the correspondence is not material to anyone. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would let the motion stand until I have had an opportunity of discussing it with him. I think we can reduce the order very materially.
The report goes on-" motion stands." In that reply the minister states that a great deal of the correspondence " is not material." Of course it is not material to anyone now except the Winnipeg Electric interests. The hon. gentleman certainly led me to believe that nothing would be done during the recess; that is the impression I gathered. The motion came up again in the house and was passed unanimously on June 6, and shortly after that parliament prorogued. From that day to the present time I have not seen these papers. A few weeks ago in this session I moved again for the correspondence and I understand that it was brought down yesterday. After the prorogation of parliament I happened to be in Orillia and I read that a bank merger was taking place, and a few weeks later the Seven

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
Sisters development was handed away over the head of the Manitoba legislature, over the heads of the people's representatives in that body and over the head of this parliament, to the Winnipeg Electric Company; and this parliament also has been treated with contempt by the government, as evidenced by their refusal to bring down the papers, and getting away with things in the recess of parliament.
At the present time the people of Manitoba and, indeed, of Canada are faced with a very grave menace to future development. It is most regrettable, now that efforts are being made to re-establish Canadian business on a firm and solid basis, that the difficulties are being multiplied in this way, and that such a basic necessity as hydro-electric power should be alienated in that province. Yet this is what the federal government is doing over the heads of the people's representatives in parliament. The federal government and the Bracken administration are jointly responsible for the unholy alliance which has been formed to give away the water-powers of Manitoba, which should be under the control of the people of that province. This government has simply handed over a vast monopoly to the Winnipeg Electric Company and the parent body, which has interests as far as the United States, Brazil and even in Tokyo. The Canadian people are no longer willing to sell its rights to private interests, and the government has no right handing out monopolies in this way without the consent of the people. As a matter of fact, it was a miracle that the Georgian bay canal deal did not go through in 1927, with Sir Clifford Sifton, Sir Herbert Holt and others who were interested. But that deal would have been consummated if the new proposed rules to be brought down were then in existence; it would have been put through if the government's new gag rules could have been applied then here in parliament.
In the present transaction millions of dollars are being handed over to a monopoly, at the expense of the people. Only the other day evidence came out to show that while there may be small deficits for the first two or three years in the development of this power by the people, yet in a short time the Winnipeg Electric Company under the present plan will be taking a million a year profit out of the pockets of the residents of Winnipeg. Generations yet unborn will suffer in consequence in their industrial, economic and domestic life. The government is simply mortgaging the labour of future generations for the benefit of a few power grabbers, and party henchmen 78594-S5.J
in Winnipeg, and this is being done, as I have said, over the heads of the people's representatives.	_
Now where is democracy while all this is going on? Where are all "the great principles of liberalism" which roll so glibly off the Prime Minister's tongue when an election campaign is on? Why, the old family compact, in the days of the struggle for responsible government, is nothing to the 1929 family compact of hon. gentlemen opposite-in their conspiracy to part with the water-powers that belong to the people of the province of Manitoba. Yesterday the Prime Minister made a speech in regard to natural resources, defending the government in relation to this question. Well, to-morrow a similar defence will be put forward in this house in regard to the Beauharnois power. But there is this difference between the old family compact and' the compact we see today: in the old days they had nothing to give away, while to-day they are giving away to favourites the rights of the people in natural resouees. We see nothing here now but every day the incapacity of the government to govern or to solve any economic problem, and the whole attitude of the government in this matter indicates the decay of parliament and the decline of the House of Commons; for over our heads they part with these resources without our consent. The economic loss and waste which we have seen in the railways out west is due directly to the insane railway policy of the Liberal party and the Grand Trunk Pacific and Crows-nest pass deals of other days. In those days the cry was "Cox can't wait," but now it is "Backus can't wait; Jones can't wait; Dafoe can't wait." Dafoe, this great pooh-bah, this king-maker who stands behdnds the throne in Ottawa and Winnipeg and pulls the strings,, can't wait; Bracken can't wait; Nesbitt can't wait, but the working classes and farmers of Manitoba can wait and will wait until doomsday before they will get any control or regulation of these rates, now that the power grabbers have won. In and out of this house the Liberal government always has been the foe of cheap light and power, not only in Ontario but in the other provinces as well, and have stood for private interests. The government of the day seem to have adopted the motto of a celebrated American, so far as the public of Manitoba are concerned, namely, "The public be damned!" The government can fool some of the people all the time and all the people some of the time but they cannot fool all the people all the time in connection with this great give-away of

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
tion a dividend on millions of dollars' worth of watered stock. I will move an amendment in a few minutes which will give the Liberals of Manitoba a chance to declare themselves.
The Minister of the Interior has mentioned the safeguards which have been put around this lease. He said it was only a temporary lease. It is a definite lease, an agreement in writing. Anyone who is familiar with the city of Winnipeg knows what a grasping, avaricious monopoly the Winnipeg Electric is. The minister says that there is control exercised over the rates; he says that the Public Utilities Commission of Manitoba, which is only the Bracken cabinet, governs the rates to be charged for light and power.

speechtext:
The Minister of the Interior is trying to use up the balance of my time. I think I know something about the city of Winnipeg; I know they own their own plant separate from the private company and have a very fine scheme of domestic lighting for the homes and domestic services and an excellent heating plant and all that. The city of Winnipeg never had a chance on this Seven Sisters grab; the city council reversed a decision they had given for public ownership of this particular Seven Sisters site. You would think you could look to the Winnipeg board of trade to do something, but you might just as well have looked to the board of trade of the city of Toronto in 1905 when the hydro got started. The Winnipeg Board of Trade would rather back the Winnipeg Electric Company than support public ownership and public control. If the cheap light and power movement in Manitoba has to depend on ministers like the Minister of the Interior, the board of trade of Winnipeg, the city council and the Liberals like the public ownership Liberals from the province of Manitoba, then it is good-bye and good-night to the cheap

light and power movement in that province. Caesar once said that all Gaul was divided into three parts. The gall of this Winnipeg electric crowd, and the Beauharnois crowd in Ottawa is so great it is absolutely indivisible.
The minister said that Doctor Hogg was sent up there to investigate this matter, but his report is almost absurd and will in time be found to have been all wrong, just as the one we had back in 1905 from Lord Kelvin when he was brought out from the old country to report on the Decew falls, near Thorold and to report on the practicability of transmitting power from Thorold to Hamilton, a little over 40 miles. He ridiculed it as an impossibility. He said that from an economic standpoint it was impossible to do it. Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck had confidence enough to start the hydro-electric system in Ontario. What was the result? Lord Kelvin said that it could not be done. He said: If you put your money in the Welland canal you can dig and you will get it out again; but if you put it into hydro, you will never get it back. Lord Kelvin was wrong; so is Doctor Hogg on the Seven Sisters matter.
I have not covered all the facts that I should like to have referred to, but I will now move my amendment. I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Gott:
That all the words after the word "That" in the motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
It be referred to the standing committee of this house on mines, forests and water-powers, to consider and investigate all leases, grants or permits issued during the past year in respect of natural resources under the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada, known as "water-powers"; with power to send for all papers and documents, to summon and examine witnesses, regarding any such leases, grants and permits.
And further, with power to the said committee to report whether such leases, grants or permits are in the public interest, and whether the interests of the federal authorities are amply protected.
And also to report whether, in the opinion of the committee, the said lease or permit in respect of the Seven Sisters falls in the province of Manitoba should be revoked and cancelled, and if so, upon what terms and conditions.
And to report all matter and findings to this house.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
In my humble opinion
the amendment is out of order, for the following reasons. Beauchesne, section 397, states:
An amendment must not raise any question which by the rules of the house, can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice.

Natural Resources-Mr. Mackenzie King
The hon. gentleman will notice that the question before the house is an abstract one.
It reads:
That in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal parliament, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
By his amendment the hon. gentleman asks, inter alia, that the lease of a specific waterpower called the Seven Sisters falls be investigated by the committee on mines, forests and water-powers. What is the procedure in this matter? I read this from Bourinot, fourth edition, page 321:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment has been proposed, and this rule has been invariably insisted upon by Canadian speakers.
Further:
If such a practice were tolerated, all the benefits of giving due notice of a motion, and allowing the house a full opportunity of considering a question, would be practically lost. A member would then be in a position to surprise the house at any moment with a motion of importance,-
This is undoubtedly a question of importance.
-and the necessity of giving notice would be superseded to all intents and purposes. It is not, therefore, surprising that the latest English decisions are in accord with those of the Canadian speakers. Sir Erskine May, in later editions, however, lays it down as "an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed."
I have on many occasions looked over precedents on the vexed question of amendments and subamendments, and the ruling is uniform on the subject that no new question must be introduced on an amendment; it must be relevant to the main question. In the present instance the resolution is an abstract one while the amendment refers to a specific subject different from the main one. I therefore rule the amendment out of order.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would you
hear just a word on that before coming to a final decision? The test, as I understand it, of the matter in accordance with the paragraph you read from Bourinot is the question: is the amendment relevant? The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
The resolution refers to the question of the natural resources under federal control and
whait disposition should be made of them. The amendment refers to the very same thing.
It deals exclusively with natural resources under federal control, proposing another way of investigation or inquiry than that proposed by the motion. Surely it is relevant to the motion whatever else may be said about it.
If it is relevant to the motion, no notice is required of such an amendment. I can understand the force of the rule that where a new question is raised irrelevant to the motion, then notice must be given and the rule must be enforced. But if the point at issue is the relevancy of the motion-and that is what Bourinot says-it refers to the identical matter and proposes merely another way of dealing with it.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister):	I entirely disagree with
my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition as to the relevancy of the amendment proposed. The amendment of the hon. member is an effort to obtain from the house a committee to investigate a particular transaction referred to more or less specifically in the last clause of his amendment. The amendment in my opinion is so framed as to appear to reflect upon the manner in which the administration has carried out its obligations with respect to certain government leases. If the hon. member has in his mind a suspicion or any ground for suspicion that in any particular the ministry has not performed its duties or any member of the ministry his duties in a befitting manner, he has the privilege, which every hon. member has, on his own responsibility to say so and to make a charge. If the hon. member on his responsibility as a member of this house will make a charge against any member of the administration, I can assure him that the government will very speedily grant him a committee; but we do not propose to have the time of parliament wasted by accepting amendments proposed by the hon. member for general inquiries which amendments are in no way relevant to the subject being discussed and which in this particular instance has to do not with parliament's investigation of one particular transaction or combination of transactions, but wholly with ratification by parliament of the disposition of aii the natural resources of the country.

His Honour the Speaker has placed the right interpretation on the motion of the hon. mem-

ber, and having regard to the authorities which His Honour has cited, the house should support his ruling. One rule cited was that:
An amendment must not raise any question which by the rules of the house, can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice.
It is certainly clear that notice should be given, in a matter of this kind, because the amendment does raise a separate and distinct question. Nor does the amendment run consecutively with any portion of the main motion, and the rule in that regard is:
