subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
When the
Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) was speaking in this debate, he mentioned that there were some Manitoba members who did not agree with the position that had been taken by the majority, and at that point the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. IV oodsworth) interjected what seemed to me to be a rather offensive remark-" Name them as though the particular members referred to were endeavouring to hide themselves and to refuse to accept responsibility for their attitude. I was one of those who did not agree with the position taken by the majority of the Manitoba members, and I was in good company. I was in company with men who were capable of taking facts, as well as theories, into consideration, men who were capable of taking into account the situation that prevailed at the time these negotiations were being entered into. I was in company with men who were just as sincerely anxious to solve this question in the interests of the people of Manitoba as were those who took the contrary view.
This is not the time nor the place to discuss the conduct of the Manitoba government. I do not conceive that this is a time to discuss the terms of the contract into which they entered, nor do I think that the extent to which any individual Manitoba member may have helped the Bracken government in the provincial election of 1927 is a matter of any great interest to this house. The question

before us is the conduct of this government and the responsibility of the minister in relation to this lease, and that, I think, is the only question that should be the subject of discussion at the present time.
The main grievance seems to have been that the minister did not to the very' last letter fulfil the obligation that he had assumed in consulting with certain Manitoba members, but it has been made clear also in the course of this debate that the minister did consult with seven of the Manitoba members. in a group, in the city of Winnipeg. It would seem, therefore, that according to the view of certain hon. members the Minister of the Interior could only have fulfilled his obligation by consulting with them. Apparently they assume that they were the ones who must be consulted, and that if they were not consulted, then the minister did not fulfil his obligation. Just at this point let me say that these same members seemed to arrogate to themselves the right to dictate the policy of this government and of this parliament, as well as that of the government and legislature of Manitoba, and of the city council of Winnipeg, and that if action were not taken by these various bodies according to their preconceived views, then that action must necessarily be wrong.
The resolution on the order paper is in very general terms, but everybody knows that it was introduced because a specific question had been brought to the attention of the public. Therefore, I propose to speak briefly as regards my own attitude towards the situation that confronted us during the last session.
Reference has been made to a round robin that was signed by the federal members from Manitoba. I do not know why they introduced that subject. It seems to me that they have made no point by introducing it. The only point that could be made was that they might urge that those who took a position contrary to the position which they themselves had taken were in some way receding from the position which was taken when that round robin was signed. Certainly we signed that document; there is no question about that. I had forgotten the exact terms of the document, but I had a fair understanding of what it meant, and I know what was in my mind when I signed it. As I understand1 it, we signed a petition addressed to the Minister of the Interior urging that when that particular lease was granted, the Manitoba government should have the first opportunity of acquiring that particular waterpower site. Having done that, I conceived that we had discharged our duty in the

Natural Resources*-Mr. Brovm
matter. It was a perfectly proper step for us to take to ask the Minister of the Interior to allow the Manitoba government to have the first say in the disposition of that power site. Not only was that my understanding of the document, but I think the terms of the document itself confirm my understanding, and show that that is all that could be read into it. The petition was addressed to the Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior, at Ottawa, and reads:
We the undersigned members of parliament from the province of Manitoba respectfully request that the power site on the Winnipeg river known as Seven Sisters falls be retained for the use of the government of the province of Manitoba in their own provincial hydro-el eetr'ic system.
That is exactly what has been done. The course that was indicated by the majority as the proper one to be taken contained three propositions: first, that the Manitoba government should have the first say as to the disposition of the power site; secondly, the Winnipeg city council, and thirdly, the Winnipeg Electric Company. But Mr. Bracken took the position that if the lease were not granted to the Winnipeg Electric Company, he was going to assert his rights and still occupy the position of priority which had been accorded to him. Now if the course that, had been advised by these other gentlemen had been followed, then when it came to granting the lease to the Winnipeg Electric Company, the Manitoba government would have had no say whatever as to the terms of that lease, nor would it have been able to enter into a contract with them, as it did.
What was the position taken by the minority of the Manitoba members? The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) has stated that he took a certain position at that time, and that he has not since changed his mind. I think perhaps some others of us can say the same, that the position which we took we deemed then, as we deem it now, to be the right one. I took this position in regard to the disposition of that site. As I have already said, when we signed that round robin, and presented it to the Minister of the Interior, I felt that we were doing our duty as representing the people of the province of Manitoba.
Having done that , I took the position that we had discharged our full duty, and that any further responsibility must rest upon the government of Manitoba, with whom the people of the province would deal when the time came. I know the Minister of the Interior did not accept as fully as I did the view that
he should act as trustee for and in accordance with the wishes of the province of Manitoba.
It will be .recalled that there had been an interprovincial conference in the fall of 1927. The announcement then made in regal'd to the objections that hitherto had been raised by the other provinces with regard to the return of these resources to the prairie provinces was sufficient I thought even at that time to warrant the government acting on the principle that they would dispose of these resources in harmony with the wishes of the government of Manitoba. So when the announcement was made following that conference, I said at once that it fully justified the position that I had taken. I think hon. members will agree that the government acting as it did following the conference with the government cf Manitoba, was simply acting in accord with the course that I had considered proper to pursue throughout the negotiations.
Now, reference has already been made to that conference. I was rather amused when the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) the other night in discussing this matter seemed more than ordinarily to attempt to overwhelm the house with a multitude of words. I could not but wonder whether he was doing what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) charged the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) with doing last session, and which he himself confessed he sometimes did, that when his argument was bad he made up for it by vigor of assertion.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
That was a confession,
made in the spirit of contrition at that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Yes. Now, we were well aware that that conference was to be held, it was a matter of public knowledge, and indeed I had special reason for knowing, due to the fact already mentioned by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) that there was a resolution on the order paper by the hon member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) dealing with the disposition of certain natural resources in the west. During the Easter recess last session I happened to get hold of a copy of the Orange Sentinel containing an article by its parliamentary correspondent, in which he indicated that this resolution might possibly prove to be embarrassing to the Progressive members from Manitoba. He said:
It will be singularly embarrassing to the Liberal-Progressive element in the house, who are all from the western provinces. They must vote for the transfer of the natural resources to their different provinces if they desire to consider the sentiment of their constituents.

Natural Resources-Mr. Brown
On the other hand, if tS*ey take that course, they will defeat the government, and they are not very keen about that. It puts them on the gridiron, and places them in a hot spot between their desire to support the government and their duty fairly to represent their constituents.
Well, to be forewarned is to be forearmed, so when I was home at Easter I called together twenty-five or thirty of my supporters and placed the situation before them. I told them there wras a possibility that the resolution by the hon. member for Frontena'c might come up an a form to involve a vote of want of confidence in the government, and I asked them how I should act under the circumstances. Well, they did not want the government to be defeated. For whatever differences there may be between the Liberals and Progressives of Manitoba, they are unanimous on one point, they do not want a Tory government. They told me they did not want to see the government defeated on that resolution, but they felt very strongly on the question of the return to the province of its natural resources. I told my supporters that according to the press there was to be a conference between the Dominion government and the government of Manitoba. They decided then that the proper course for me to pursue, if the matter came up in the form I suggested was that if I could get an assurance from the Prime Minister that the proposed conference would take place, then I might vote against the resolution of the hon. member for Frontenac, involving as it would a vote of want of confidence in the government. That resolution was not proceeded with. I was sorry for I wished to show how we would act when placed on the gridiron. I mention that because of the discussion which has arisen in regard to that conference. It was a matter of public knowledge, and I had an assurance from the Prime Minister that the conference would be held. The result of the conference was entirely satisfactory to me.
It has been said that when the agreement was made following that conference the Seven Sisters site should have been made an exception. I cannot understand how anyone could make such a suggestion. In a conference of that kind where it was agreed that the natural resources should be handled in harmony with the wishes of the government of Manitoba, it would have been absolutely absurd to make an exception with regard to one particular case. It is true that Premier Bracken in his negotiations held a position to the disadvantage of those who took the other view, but none the less they must accept the position as they find it. I have not
IMr. Brown.]
the slightest doubt that if the question of the return of the natural resources to Manitoba had come up at an earlier stage of last session, and if such a method of dealing with (them had (been suggested, every member would have voted in favour of the course adopted, and probably would have resented the suggestion that any exception at all should be made.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose at this time to deal with the terms of the contract made by the Manitoba government. That is a matter for which that government is responsible to its own people, and they alone have the right to decide the question. As an elector of Manitoba I propose when the time comes to deal with the question according to my best judgment, just as I try to deal with the questions that come before this house, and I do not think anything is gained by introducing irrelevancies that have not the slightest bearing on the matter in hand.
I propose to vote against the resolution. I have heard it suggested that an amendment might be moved limiting the scope of the resolution to water-power. The suggested amendment has not yet been moved. I cannot vote for any resolution or amendment -that would in any way have the effect of qualifying the agreement that was made between this government and the government of Manitoba that the resources should be handled by this government in harmony with the wishes of the provincial government.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the
Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) stated that after communicating with as many members from Manitoba as he could reach during the summer, he found that the opposition which had been so evident here last session was largely removed. In view of that statement, and in order to put my position clearly on record, I feel it my duty to say that my opposition to the leasing of the Seven Sisters falls power site to private interests continued from first to last. I know that was the position also of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. McDiarmid). In fact, all of the members in this house from the city of Winnipeg, whether Liberal or Labour, were united in their opposition to the transaction from the beginning to the end, and I am not aware of the slightest wavering on the part of a single one of them.
The various step3 that were taken in connection with this whole controversy have been enumerated, and I shall not deal with them in detail. The first document which I placed

Natural Resources-Mr. Thorson
on my file in connection with, the matter-and I have a very voluminous file on the subject- is a copy of the letter dated February 8, addressed to the Minister of the Interior and signed by every single private member from Manitoba in this house. We all signed that document thinking that we were supporting and furthering the wishes of the government of Manitoba.
The next event of importance in connection with the transaction was the announcement which appeared in the press on March 22, 1928. The announcement as it appeared in the Manitoba Free Press of that day is as follows:
Abandons Scheme for Development at Seven Sisters
Will purchase supply from Winnipeg Electric Company at $13.80 per horse-power on thirty-year agreement
Abandoning its scheme for the development of the Seven Sisters falls site, as a public ownership enterprise, in consequence of the unfavourable report submitted by Dr. T. A. Hogg, Ontario power expert, the provincial government has entered into a contract with the Winnipeg Electric railway for the supply of
30,000	horse-power for 30 years at $13.80 per horse-power.
As a result of the agreement the company will at once proceed with a $15,000,000 power development scheme at the Seven Sisters falls.
I will say quite frankly that this announcement, coming so soon after the previous request of the Manitoba government, came upon us like a thunderbolt, in view of the previous attitude taken by the Manitoba legislature and the Manitoba government with regard to the Seven Sisters falls power site.
The controversy then began to rage at Ottawa. The Minister of the Interior asked the opinion of the Manitoba members with regard to the application of the private company. We were bombarded in the usual way with letters, telegrams, and resolutions passed by various bodies and organizations both for and against the application of the private company for a lease of the power site. The Manitoba members held several meetings to discuss the matter and during the Easter recess a committee of their number went to Winnipeg to study the situation there. I was not a member of that committee but I had already advised the Minister of the Interior of my opposition to the application made by the private company.
On May 15 the Manitoba members held their final meeting in connection with the matter, and I am quite free to admit that it was a very stormy one. A letter was drafted and sent to the Minister of the Interior advising him of the views of the majority of the
Manitoba members. I was one of the majority who voted for delay in granting the application that was under consideration. The terms of the letter addressed to the Minister of the Interior have already been placed on Hansard and I need not refer to them further.
On May 25 a very large delegation came from Winnipeg, many members of which were political and personal friends of my own, urging that the lease be granted immediately. That delegation met a committee of the cabinet in the morning, and in the afternoon there was a meeting of the Winnipeg delegates, the Minister of the Interior and several of the Manitoba members. I was one of the members present at that meeting, and nothing that I heard on that occasion caused me in any way to change the opinion I had formed.
Reference has also been made to the statement made by the Minister of the Interior on the floor of this house in reply to a question put forward by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The statement of the minister is on Hansard and has already been referred to in the course of this debate. It is very wide in its terms: I must confess that the letter which was read this afternoon by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) comes as a shock to me. After the Minister of the Interior had made his statement on the floor of the house he gave us privately to understand that he would take no action in connection with the application for the lease until he had consulted further with the Manitoba members. That is the position in which the matter was left at the close of the 1928 session of parliament, which prorogued on June 13.
The right of the Manitoba members to intervene in the matter was freely challenged at the time, both editorially and in a resolution that was drafted by the persons who had arranged the Winnipeg delegation. That resolution was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) ; it was obviously drafted in heat and lacked that calm deliberation which a resolution of that sort should have shown. I therefore make no further reference to it. I should like, however, to say a few words with regard to the question of responsibility for the administration of the natural resources of Manitoba. At the meeting with the members of the Winnipeg delegation, to which I have already referred, I took the view that we, as federal members, owed a duty to our constituencies in the matter and that we would discharge that duty in the best interests of our constituencies and not in the

Natural Resources-Mr. Thorson
interests of any groups or organizations; I took the view that we would discharge that duty in accordance with our best judgment. At that time there was no doubt whatsoever that the responsibility for dealing with the natural resources of Manitoba and with the application that was before the federal government for consideration lay primarily with the Minister of the Interior and the federal government. That fact was recognized by Premier Bracken himself in the communication which he addressed to the federal government. He had not expressed any desire to assume responsibility for granting the application of the private company; in fact, he had indicated in his letters that the responsibility for granting the application was solely that of the federal government. In his letter of March 22 he says:
I am writing you at this time to say that a satisfactory arrangement has been arrived at and that as soon as the details of our understanding are embodied in a contract between the Winnipeg Electric Company and the provincial government we shall be in a position to advise you that we shall withdraw our application for the lease of this site so as to leave the way open for such negotiation as may be necessary between the Winnipeg Electric Company and yourselves concerning the lease of the site.
The granting of the lease was to be made a matter of negotiation between the Winnipeg Electric Company and the federal government. Then he wrote again on April 25, as follows:
We are writing you now to advise you that a tentative contract between the Winnipeg Electric Company and the provincial government has been agreed upon, and that once you decide to lease the site to them you may disregard our application for the same. If for any reason, however, you should decide not to lease the site to the Winnipeg Electric Company, after all these negotiations, we desire our application to stand, since equally favourable terms must be secured to the provincial government from any other company securing the lease before we would relinquish our prior claim to it.
The question of where the responsibility lay agitated the minds of others. The Manitoba Free Press of May 26, the day after the Winnipeg delegation arrived in Ottawa, contained an editorial entitled "Where Responsibility Lies," the first paragraph of which contained the following:
The facts as to where power and responsibility lie in the granting of the right to make use of our natrual resources can be briefly stated. These resources belong to the crown as represented by the federal authority. Under the regulations, adopted by the Dominion government, the power of granting rights to cut timber or pulpwod, to develop mines or water-powers, rests with the Minister of the Interior. 
It is, of course, the right of anyone interested to make representations to the minister. He can listen to their representations and^ give effect to them if he chooses; but the decision is his and the responsibility is his.
Further on the editorial contains this statement:
Any claim which may be made by members of parliament from Manitoba that they have the right to decide is sheer pretention. They have neither a veto nor a directive powrer over the minister. What he does, he does on his own responsibility.
On his own responsibility to whom? His responsibility is not to any provincial government but to this parliament, of which we are the members most interested. If the minister is not responsible to the members of this parliament, to whom is he responsible? We were not seeking in any way to assert any right to decide the matter in our capacity as private members of parliament. Under our system of government decision with respect to matters of this nature rests with the cabinet who, I would remind the house, occupy the positions which they d'o because the people of Canada have seen fit to send more members to this side of the house than to the other. The responsibility for their decision in this matter, as in all executive matters, is to this house. Should we, who had been expressly asked for our opinions in the matter, have refused to give them? Each Manitoba member gave his opinion, I believe, in the honest and sincere discharge of the responsibilities which he in turn owed to the electors of his own constituency. I am not impugning the motives of a single Manitoba member. On June 2, 1928, the Free Press contained a further editorial entitled:
The Extent of the Bracken Government Responsibility.
The last paragraph of that editorial is as follows:
The Manitoba government, by its action in withdrawing its application, left the field clear for the Winnipeg Street Railway to press its application at Ottawa; but it did not thereby, as many of its critics insist, turn Seven Sisters falls over to the street railway. It has not even made recommendations to that effect. It is for Mr. Stewart to say whether the application is to be granted or not. His liberty of decision in this respect is not in the least limited by what has been done by the Bracken government.
Up to that time there had been no suggestion on the part of the Manitoba government that the Minister of the Interior necessarily must act as the government of Manitoba might desire him to do and the Minister of the Interior admitted in this house that the responsibility was his.

Natural Resources-Mr. Thorson
This, then, was the situation when we left Ottawa at the close of last session. We who were urging that the lease should not be granted were attempting to assist the government in discharging their responsibilities in accordance with what we thought was in the best interests of the constituencies we represented.
Upon my return, to Winnipeg I made a public statement as to my stand in the matter on June 26, at a dinner given in my honour by some of my constituents. In order that I may place my stand on record I now read what I said on that occasion:
I would not be doing justice to my constituency or to myself if I failed to say a few words with regard to the Seven Sisters falls controversy and the stand which I took. On February 8, the 16 private members from Manitoba signed a letter addressed to the Hon. Charles Stewart requesting that the Seven Sisters power site be retained for the use of the province of Manitoba, notwithstanding the fact that there was a previous application from the Winnipeg Electric Company for the site. In so acting we were seeking to preserve what we all conceived to be the public interest of the province. The name of every single member from Manitoba, with the exception of the Hon. Robert Forke, is attached to that letter.
Naturally we were astonished when the agreement was signed between the province and the Winnipeg Electric Company and the application of the company was presented.
The responsibility for dealing with the application rested, as it still does, with Hon. Charles Stewart and the Dominion government. Mr. Stewart has adopted the practice in the past two years of consulting with the Manitoba members on matters affecting the disposal of natural resources in Manitoba. That policy worked well in the past, particularly in connection with the establishment of our great pulp and paper industry at Pine falls. That industry was established in spite of vigorous protests from several Winnipeg sources. I had an active share in the preliminary negotiations with the government here.
In pursuance of his practice Mr. Stewart asked the opinion of the Manitoba members as to what action should be taken on the application before him. We discussed the matter at several meetings, studied the question to the best of our ability with the information which was available to us.
On May 15, when we held a meeting at which we finally reached a decision, there were four members in favour of granting the application immediately and 10 against. I was one of the 10. Of the 10 members there were four Liberal, three Liberal Progressives, two Labour and one Progressive. Seven sit on the government side of the house and three with the opposition.
I mention these facts merely to show that the question was not one of party politics at Ottawa and it is not a political question in this city.
When I add that the city council is almost evenly divided on the matter and that six out of the 10 members from Winnipeg in the
provincial legislature are in favour of delay and full consideration of the question, I think you will agree that there is a strong difference of opinion. I also suggest that it is possible for all these representatives elected by the people in various capacities to hold the views they do without being either fools or knaves. It seems the lot of public men to suffer abuse. I realize that fact, but I do not intend to deviate from the discharge of my responsibilities through fear of personal abuse and am prepared to submit to it, if necessary, in the discharge of my public duties.
I voted against the granting of the application because I believed it was not in the public interest to grant it. I did not wish to stand in the way of development, but unless it was demonstrated to me that it was necessary to grant this valuable site to private interests for development, I did not wish that to be done. I felt also that the grant of this site to the Winnipeg Electric Company would place the Winnipeg hydro at a serious disadvantage and would endanger its future.
At present we have an ideal situation in Winnipeg, two concerns handling power, one publicly, the other privately owned, each acting as a check on the other and each controlling a substantial block of power. The Winnipeg hydro has 138.000 horse-power at Point du Bois and the Winnipeg Electric 205,000 at Great falls and Pinawa.
I was riot convinced, and am not now convinced, that the shortage of power is so acute that it is essential to turn the site over to a private concern. Granting the site to the Winnipeg Electric Company would leave our great power asset 30 per cent in the hands of the public and 70 per cent in private hands. That in my opinion, would be fraught with serious danger.
If there is no available market for power developed by the province, there is no immediate need for development by the Winnipeg Electric.
We are told that the present horse-power resources will be exhausted in two years. I doubt the accuracy of that statement. If the provincial government or the city of Winnipeg are not prepared to develop the Seven Sisters site then I am in favour of development along the following lines:
The Winnipeg hydro to develop Slave Falls and the Winnipeg Electric McArthur Falls. That would give 228,000 horse-power to the former and 259.000 horse-power to the latter. That process of development, even admitting the statement as to power shortage, would amply provide for power needs for at least six years and would maintain an even balance between the two systems, a consideration which I deem highly desirable.
By that time the development at Pine Falls must take place and an additional block of power amounting to 111,000 horse-power would be available.
The Seven Sisters site should be used as a reservoir from which the two competing systems could draw. In my opinion it would be profitable and sound business for the province to develop the Seven Sisters site in the future when the power situation requires it, with this situation in mind; either to go into the power business or preferably to sell to the competing systems in large blocks as required for distribution by them.
558	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Thorson
It is profitable for the Winnipeg Electric to do this now. Why should it not also be profitable for the province? This wholesale business would be profitable in itself and would serve as a profitable basis for extension of the system elsewhere if it should be deemed advisable.
We must remember that the province outside of Winnipeg has rights in the matter which must be considered.
The situation at Pinawa could be easily met by allotting to the Winnipeg Electric a reasonable block of power in return for closing up the Pinawa channel. In my opinion the Winnipeg Electric would be glad to come to such an arrangement if the control of Seven Sisters was in the hands of the province.
We have had many battles in the past over the Winnipeg river and we have reaped the rewards of vigilance and foresight. Waterpower is too vital an asset to hand over without careful deliberation and I see nothing but value in a thorough airing of this controversy.
It is not pleasant for those around whom it centres, but that is of minor importance. The essential thing it that the best interests of the public must be safeguarded.
I have stated very briefly my reasons for taking the stand which I did and I see no cause for receding from it. It was no easy matter to come to a decision in view of the differences of opinion, the pressure that was brought to bear and the threats that were made. Each member, when he voted as he did, took tile responsibility for his decision on his own shoulders. I am not seeking to have this meeting endorse my views. Mr. Robson has his views on the matter and many of my best friends are opposed to me on this question. They are entitled to their opinions.
I am not vain enough to claim infallibility of judgment. Time alone will tell whether my attitude was right or wrong. I think it was right and I shall face the responsibility for my actions when the time comes.
Then came the natural resources agreement between the Manitoba government and the Dominion government. I will deal with the natural resources agreement a little later. Personally I cannot complain that I was not consulted by the Minister of the Interior. It is true that I was not consulted until after the natural resources agreement had been arrived at, but subsequently to the date of that agreement I was consulted on several occasions. I think it is only fair to the minister to say that. He saw me on July 6, if I remember correctly, but he could not have taken away from the interview we had then the belief that my opposition had weakened in any way. He saw several of us again in Winnipeg in the month of August, and my impression of that meeting was that there had been no change in the attitude of the members present at that meeting with the possible exception of one member. I had not altered in any manner the position which I had previously taken regarding this matter. On September 5, learning that it was likely that the matter would be finally dealt with by the 
cabinet, I wired to Ottawa stating that the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. McDiarmid) and myself were strongly opposed to the granting of the lease, and asking for an opportunity to appear before the cabinet to present our views. After the natural resources agreement was entered into between the province of Manitoba and the Dominion of Canada the question of the responsibility for administering the resources of Manitoba took on a different complexion. Premier Bracken, who a short time before had requested that the Seven Sisters falls power site should be reserved for the province of Manitoba, now insisted that under the terms of the natural resources agreement, and more particularly clause 6 of that agreement, the Dominion government should grant the lease to the private company immediately. I believe there was quite a lengthy correspondence between the provincial government and federal government with regard to the subject; in fact the correspondence amounted almost to a barrage. Before the lease was signed the federal government insisted on an order in council from the Manitoba government, and the Manitoba government finally passed an order in council directing the federal government to issue the lease as set out therein. Finally the lease was granted at the insistence of Premier Bracken.
In putting forward the opposition which I did both before and after the natural resources agreement was entered into. I was acting in what I believed to be the best interests of the people who had sent me to parliament. I was convinced that the majority of the electors in my constituency were opposed to the granting of this lease to private interests. I took the view that so long as the lease was not. actually signed there was still hope of saving the Seven Sisters falls from going into private hands-but stronger forces prevailed.

of the province of Manitoba should be definitely settled and one authority given control over them.
However, I have this to say in connection with the natural resources agreement: there has been a fundamental change in the policy of this government as to the administration of the natural resources of the province of Manitoba. Prior to the making of the natural resources agreement in July last, the federal government took the view that the responsibility for administering the natural resources lay with it, and that it was not bound by the wishes of the Manitoba government. It did not follow in all respects the wishes of the Manitoba government in connection with the matter. An outstanding example of that is to be found in the manner in which the Minister of the Interior and the federal government dealt with the pulp and paper proposition of two years ago, to which I referred in my speech at Winnipeg. The federal government did not accept the advice of the provincial government in respect of that transaction and it had never formally recognized the right of the provincial government to dictate to it what its policy of administration of the resources of the province should be. It had of course followed the policy of consulting the province of Manitoba in respect of the larger matters but it had reserved the right of deciding for itself whether it would follow the wishes of the province or not.
When the natural resources agreement was entered into there was a vital change in the policy that had been followed prior to that time; for, in pursuance of clause 6 of the agreement, the federal government has constituted itself merely the agent of the provincial government to administer the resources according to the wishes of the provincial government and it has definitely and formally recognized its position as a trustee. Perhaps this is as it should be, but I have this criticism to make: the first five clauses of the natural resources agreement carry with them the implication that they shall not go into effect until they have been ratified by parliament. I should perhaps state that in a different way-that the final transfer of the resources shall not be effective until the findings of the commission set up have been ratified by parliament, but there is no proviso of that sort with regard to clause 6 of the agreement. Immediately and automatically on the making of that agreement, the responsibility of the Dominion government for administering the resources is changed. I have this criticism to make, namely, that the change in policy was
so vital that it should not have become effective until ratified by parliament, and that a rider should have been attached to clause 6 of the natural resources agreement to the effect that until the fundamental change in the policy of administering the resources had been approved by parliament, the change of policy indicated by clause 6 should not go into effect.
In view of the differences of opinion that existed in this house; in view of the differences of opinion that existed in Manitoba; in view of the undertaking which the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) gave on the floor of this house, and in view of the developments that have taken place, I think it would have been a wise course to follow to take the view that before this' fundamental change in the policy of administering the natural resources of Manitoba should come into effect, it should be ratified by parliament. That would have been in the interests of all concerned here; it would certainly have been in the interests of the government of Manitoba which finds itself in such difficulties to-day.
I have been very glad to associate myself with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), and all the other members of this house who opposed the granting of the lease to private interests; but notwithstanding my opposition to the transaction I cannot agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the mover of this resolution, as to the terms of his resolution. The argument of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the resolution appears to me almost unanswerable. It is impossible, in my opinion, to assign to parliament the executive functions of government. The business of administration could not go on if every disposal of property should, before becoming effective, be ratified by parliament. There is a further reason for my objection to the general terms of the resolution. I do not believe we should endeavour in this country unduly to restrict the executive. nor do I think we should attempt to develop a water-tight sytem of compartments of responsibility'. It is of the essence of our constitution that it should be elastic; that it should be based upon confidence and trust, and that as few restrictions as possible should be imposed upon those responsible for government. The electors of Canada send us to parliament with wide powers; having expressed their confidence in us, the will of the electors also determines from which party in this house the cabinet shall be formed and who shall be charged with the responsibility
560	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Howden
for executive acts. The resolution seeks to remove from the jurisdiction of the executive powers which are not legislative but executive. I do not believe that in the long run, much as it would have assisted us in this particular case, it would be in the interest of sound government to adopt the resolution. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is to be congratulated upon having made this motion and upon having discussed this very important question here. It will have served the very useful purpose of reminding the government of its responsibility to parliament. While executive acts must be performed by those appointed for the purpose, they are responsible for their executive acts to parliament. No cabinet in any British country should be allowed to forget for one moment that responsibility. I have fought the Seven Sisters falls power lease to the best of my ability; I have been opposed to the granting of the lease from the beginning to the end, but for the reasons I have given I cannot see my way clear to approving the resolution that is now before this house.

I have your letter of the 31st ultimo re the Seven Sisters falls lease, together with the memorandum of statements made in your legislature about the matter. As the matter is one that has created a great deal of interest in Manitoba and last night was made the matter of comment in the house by the hon. Mr. Bennett and, in view of the fact that delay of a. momth or so will not injure the prospects of this development, I think it wise on my part to delay the issuing of the license for that time.	'
However, I note you have not changed your position from that taken in your former letter.
Yours,
Charles Stewart.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the whole method of dealing with these matters has been wrong, and that we should be on the safe side in respect of an important matter like water powers by first obtaining the judgment of this house. The right hon. the Prime Minister said that the Navigable Waters Protection Act contained a provision which permitted the annulment of any permit issued under that act. Such a provision stands in the face of the men who have put money into an enterprise, who obtain a permit from the department and they are always faced with the fact that such permit may be annnulled ten years afterwards, but the whole thing is so unfair that it has never been acted upon and I cannot imagine a case where it would be acted upon. I intend to move an amendment whereby such important matters shall be returned to the house for its ratification before they go into effect. The Minister of the Interior did not think that a delay of a month or so would make any difference in a matter of this kind, indeed I submit it will not make any difference if there is a delay of
six months or a year until such matters are ratified by the parliament of Canada. No harm will be done but only good, because the people will see how these major resources, these water powers, are being dealt with by the government of the day. We feel that the provision proposed to be inserted tin the Navigable Waters Protection Act should properly be in that act. I agree with the Prime Minister when he says that we cannot clog up the business in this house by passing on every little transaction. We do not insist that every homestead and that sort of thing should be returned to this house to get the ratification of parliament, and until that ratification had been given should have no effect. I do not think that is necessary, and in that regard I think the resolution of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) goes too far, although the principle is good if applied in the proper way. When a water-power site like this one is given away it is diverting from the people of the country their rightful heritage. It is the natural run of water as nature left it and no private person should have that to the exclusion of benefits which should accrue to the people. We could split the resolution at that point, and I propose to move an amendment which will have that effect.
I judge from the utterances of the Prime Minister that we are on the eve of seeing a permit granted to the Beauharnois people. He said that the engineers must certify that any development will not interfere with navigation. Before we finished the session last year we had a discussion on the St. Lawrence waterway, and this much came from that discussion: that we must consult the premiers of the two provinces concerned, Quebec and Ontario, and we must seek to have reconciled the conflicting views of the engineers in regard to the development. These engineers have not met; they have not reconciled those conflicting views, and in the absence of such reconciliation, and in the absence of those engineers saying the development can be proceeded with, I think we are making a grave error in doing anything with the power sites on the St. Lawrence river until a full agreement has been arrived at by the engineers. These matters should be settled with regard to the whole stretch from lake Ontario to Montreal before we attempt to interfere with one part of it. Like most of the members I have been listening off and on to this discussion for two or three days, a discussion of a most extraordinary nature on a most extraordinary subject. Coming from western Canada I have been accustomed there to take pride in the growth of that part of the country, developed as it has been under the policies of successive federal governments, of disposing-alienating is the word that would be used to-day-of certain natural resources of those sections, which have existed there since the dawn of creation. Those lands were not worth twenty-eight million dollars, they were not worth a nickel, until men came in and brought them under cultivation. But, as I have said, we had become accustomed to the wonderful growth of that western country under the policy adopted, and adopted wisely, a generation or two ago by this parliament and adhered to during the intervening years. What was that policy? That the government of this country, under legislation passed by parliament, was empowered to alienate the resources of the prairie provinces, to give them to individuals, to lease or sell them to cor-7S594-37
porations, with the result that to-day that western country upholds the trade and financial credit of the Dominion in the markets of the world. And yet the policy under which that tremendous development has taken place is attacked to-night by the original motion, and in a milder form by the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, had the policy which is now being proposed been in effect during the last thirty or forty years would western Canada to-day be supporting millions of people, would we have the great cities of Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, would we see the railways strung across from the lakes and over the Rocky mountains to the Pacific seaboard? Such a development would have been impossible if every homestead application had to be passed on in this house, and if hon. members wanted to know why John Jones should get a certain quarter-section, and required that the application and all the correspondence and other papers relating thereto should be placed on the table of this house. But that is exactly what would have happened if the principle of this resolution had been in force. For a copy of all letters, telegrams, _ correspondence, and any other documents in the possession of the government or any department thereof, in connection with the sale of section 26, township 32, range 32, west of the first meridian.
This motion for a copy of documents relates, it will be noticed, to the sale of a section of land. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) wants to know all the details; but if that land and other resources had been given away you can imagine the number of inquiries that would appear on the order paper, and it is safe to assume that this house would find it very difficult to discharge its functions as a branch of parliament. The policy under which western Canada has been developed has been almost uniformly successful, experience has shown it to be wise, and it would be a sad state of affairs if it were displaced by the policy now proposed.
I remember the leader of the opposition speaking very feelingly about the officers of the Department of the Interior. I should like to pay a tribute to the department not only since the present minister has been in charge but since its inception. Since the prairie ' provinces began to grow settlers have looked to the Minister of the Interior and to the officers of his department as their friends.

If the water-powers in western Canada, for instance, are not rightfully under the control of the federal government that government could not dispose of them now. And if the lands and other resources still under the control of the federal government should not be disposed of by the Department of the Interior, I cannot see how the hon. member for Frontenac can justify his change of front. I should just like to point out what the passing of this resolution would mean. I admit that if the amendment passes it would not have all the effect that I am about to describe. What would have been the effect on the men who were depending for their living on the cutting of that timber?
Now, a new thought has struck me-does the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) interrupt?-the hon. gentleman who was so busy telling the house three years ago that the extremely hard conditions in his city had forced hundreds of working men to go out in the depths of the Canadian winter and pull grass off the mountain for fuel, and that those hard conditions were due to tariff reductions? There is a point in connection with this matter which I think the hon. member who pro-posed the resolution has overlooked. It is not asked that the disposition of lands shall be ratified by this house; it is proposed that it shall be ratified by parliament. Now, without saying anything derogatory, which would bring down on myself the wrath of the Chair, everyone knows that the other part of parliament, of which I must speak respectfully, has not always seen eye to eye with this house. Many times legislation passed by this house has received the cold shoulder in the other chamber, and now are we going to ask that no development shall be allowed in the western provinces, which, generally speaking, have been under the administration of the Dominion government- under the control of the Department of the Interior and to some extent of the Department of Fisheries-until the consent not only of this house but of the other also has been obtained? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
house entered upon the debate on the address hon. gentlemen opposite, through the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) spent some time in criticizing the government on the delay in the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces. Since the present government came into office* we have been doing out utmost to hasten this transfer believing that the western provinces were justified in desiring the return of their resources at the earliest possible moment. What is the one reason above all others which has occasioned this desire on the part of the western provinces for the speedy transfer of their resources? Water-power to-day is coming to have a significance in industrial development which it has never had heretofore in the history of this country. The people of western Canada, appreciating that fact and realizing what it means to have possession of their water-powers, are anxious to have those water-powers under their own control to further in the manner they think best the industrial development of their provinces. What is the position being taken in this parliament this evening? The hon. the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), who comes'from the province of Ontario which is

highly industrialized through the development of electric, power, introduces a motion which absolutely divides eastern and western Canada; which says in so many words that while the older provinces of Ontario and Quebec may have all the freedom they wish to develop their natural resources, and to develop their water-powers in particular, the western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are not to be permitted to have any industrial development dependent upon electric energy developed from water-power until the particular plans and sites and all transactions incidental to the transfer of their water-powers and to their development are approved by this parliament.
Parliament is made up of two houses, the House of Commons and the Senate. Hon. gentlemen opposite still have a majority in the senate, and the industrial development of western Canada is to be made dependent upon the will of a Tory majority in the senate. That in effect is the result of the amendment-before this house at the present time. I am somewhat surprised that my hon. friend (Mr. Woodswoirth) who is a bit of a radical, is prepared to put his province in a position where its industrial development will depend upon ratification of the majority in the senate. The amendment reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house no disposition of the water-powers under the control of the federal government shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
That does not mean the water-powers in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Ontario or British Columbia, but it does mean all of the water-powers in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, because those water-powers are under the control of this government pending their actual transfer to the western provinces. This government has entered into an agreement with the government of one of these western provinces, and one of the conditions of that agreement is that its natural resources, including its water-powers, are to be administered in accordance with the wishes of that province from the time the agreement was made until the province is actually in full possession and control of its resources. Is the spectacle not an amusing one for us to be asked by a member from that particular province, of all parts, to break that contract and all that is implied in it? This contract provides for the trans-

Natural Resources-Mr. Evans
fer of the control of all the resources, not only one particular resource. The Manitoba government stressed its desire to have all its resources administered in accordance with its own wishes, and so far as the resources were concerned I remember particular emphasis being laid in our conferences upon the effect the explorations in northern Manitoba today would be likely to have on future industrial development. A development such as we have not seen in Canada before may be expected in a very short time, in Alberta or Saskatchewan as well as in Manitoba, but as has been mentioned by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McLean, Melfort), industrial development is something that has to be proceeded with rapidly or it will in many cases fail altogether. What is true of Manitoba is equally true of Saskatchewan and Alberta. So far as the government is concerned we have made a contract, on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, with one of the provinces of the west, and we have promised to make similar contracts with the two other provinces. This government will not begin a great policy of transferring the natural resources by contractual agreement, a policy which tends to unite this country from coast to coast more firmly than ever, by breaking one contract at its very inception.
The most serious issue that can be raised in this country is the issue of provincial rights, and that question is raised the moment any province is told that it cannot do what it likes with its own but must wait for the ratification of this parliament. The transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces has been delayed for one reason, among others, namely, because the proposed agreement stipulated in effect that the provinces were to be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of the Dominion as far as their natural resources were concerned. Those words seemed to be fair enough, but it was alleged by the western provinces that they admitted of debate, and that there was doubt as to what they might mean. The province of Manitoba alleged that it might be necessary to get an interpretation as to their exact significance from the privy council. This government took the position that the right thing to do was to say that we believed the western provinces should be put as nearly as possible in exactly the position they would have been in had they had their resources from the moment they were created as provinces. That is the position we have taken in this new agreement; it admits of no debate or doubt, and having taken that position we intend to stand by it. We intend to see that the western provinces obtain their natural resources on a basis which will put them, so far as may now be possible, in the position they would have been in had they had the administration of their natural resources from the time they were created as provinces, and that means the right of their governments and legislatures, not our parliament, to decide what is to be done.
I think we have discussed this question long enough. There are many arguments that might be urged, but I do submit that when we have such a great issue as the question of the rights of the provinces as against the Dominion raised in an amendment; when we have an issue created which tends to divide eastern Canada from western Canada; when we have an amendment which threatens to hold back the industrial development of a large part of this Dominion to which the rest of the Dominion is already widely indebted, we should not waste very much time in letting the country know where we stand in regard to it.

For many years past, organized agriculture has from time to time declared its views in this matter by adopting resolutions something in these words. I hold in my hand what is known as the farmers' platform, on which the whole Progressive party that occupied this part of the house after 1921 was elected. The resolution reads:	[DOT]
The council recommends that no more of the natural resources be alienated from the crown, but that these be brought into use only under short-term leases in which the interests of the public shall be properly safeguarded, and that such leases be granted only by public auction.
I am sure the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will remember this resolution as well as some of the discussions which took place before the Canadian Council of Agriculture. More than that on many occasions my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown), as president, put this resolution before his own organization. I cannot understand the action of men to-day in dealing with this matter. The action of the Liberal party and of the Conservative party on this question has been a mystery to me for many, many years.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Has not the hon. member also been a little mystified occasionally by the action of the Progressive party? I think he will admit that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman can think that too if he likes. But whatever was the excuse in 1870 for the passing of the Dominion Lands Act, when responsible government was created in Rupert's Land and the northwest territory there was no need for the Dominion government to withhold those resources from their rightful owners. Had there been any
excuse even for that, surely when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were created we should have been placed on an equal status with the rest of the Dominion. Why mince matters any longer? There is one faction on that side and one faction on this.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
